<reason>Both sides argued at a high level, but PRO (B) answered the decisive pressures more concretely. CON's central dilemma — that funded support must be either conditioned (boardroom colonialism) or unconditioned (mere aid) — was rhetorically sharp, but PRO resolved it with a real mechanism: a finite, recipient-directed endowment whose interest prices ongoing costs once, plus the distinction that an obligation is defined by irrevocability, not by conditions. That structure simultaneously answered CON's perpetual-budget, one-time-damages, and who-certifies-adequacy attacks, and PRO's closing ("a duty you cannot revoke is not a gift you cannot refuse") directly closed the loop. PRO's "underfunded, not incompetent" reversal and "empty toolbox" reframe also blunted the colonial-slur charge effectively. CON's certification point and "patronage with better manners" framing landed hard, and the Egypt example and sovereign-choice argument were solid, but CON increasingly asserted the dilemma rather than dismantling PRO's endowment answer. CON's clipped opening adds a small execution cost. PRO holds the stronger, more mechanized path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange over damages and the endowment: CON argued damages are one-time payments to a specific owner, and that perpetual conservation budgets denominated in the funder's "capacity" recreate hierarchy. PRO's response — a polluter endowing lifetime medical monitoring prices future harm once, and an obligation is about why one must pay, not what one may command — was the most direct, mechanism-backed answer of the debate and blunted CON's strongest line.</best_rebuttal>
